notes.title: -나 봐요
notes.text: -나 봐요 (verbs) and -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 (adjectives) are guesses based on what you see or hear: 밖에 비가 오나 봐요 (It must be raining — people have umbrellas). 피곤한가 봐요 (You must be tired). On the phone: 여보세요 (hello), 전화를 끊다 (hang up), 잘못 걸었어요 (wrong number).

notes.title: -는지
notes.text: -는지 (verbs) and -(으)ㄴ지 (adjectives and nouns) tuck a question inside a sentence: 어디 사는지 알아요? (Do you know where she lives?) 누구인지 몰라요 (I don't know who it is). It loves verbs like 알다, 모르다, 궁금하다 (to wonder) and 찾아보다 (to look up).

notes.title: Reading the news
notes.text: 기사 = article, 제목 = headline, 내용 = content, 신문사 = newspaper company. Korean headlines drop verbs and particles and often end in a noun: 웹툰의 새 스타, 한별 ("Webtoons' New Star: Han Byeol"). Written Korean also uses the plain -다 ending: 태어났다 = "was born."

notes.title: -(으)ㄹ지
notes.text: -(으)ㄹ지 is for uncertain future things: 비가 올지 모르겠어요 (I don't know if it'll rain). Pair opposites for "whether … or …": 갈지 안 갈지 (whether or not to go), 슬퍼할지 기뻐할지 (whether she'll be sad or glad).

lessons.goal: Talk about TV, media and ads.

notes.title: TV words
notes.text: 방송 = broadcast, 방송국 = station, 채널 = channel, 시청자 = viewers, 광고 = ads. 프로 is short for 프로그램 (a TV show: 요리 프로, 예능 프로) and also means "a pro." Taxi drivers are politely called 기사님.
